newsitem.title: USA: Accused Unabomber may challenge seized evidence.
newsitem.headline: Accused Unabomber may challenge seized evidence.

text.p: A judge has given lawyers for accused Unabomber Theodore Kaczynski permission to make a new bid to exclude evidence seized during a search of Kaczynski's Montana cabin, court papers showed on Tuesday.

But U.S. District Judge Garland Burrell said in an order filed on Monday that prosecutors could use Kaczynski's private diaries as evidence against him at a trial scheduled to begin in November, rejecting a defence motion to exclude them.
Kaczynski, a reclusive former mathematics professor, is accused of being the shadowy Unabomber who killed three people and injured 23 during an anti-technology bombing campaign between 1978 and 1995.

Kaczynski has been charged in Sacramento with four bombings, two of them deadly, and could face the death penalty if convicted. He was arrested in Montana last year and has pleaded not guilty to the charges.

Last month, Burrell denied a motion by Kaczynski's lawyers to throw out evidence seized by the FBI during an April 1996 search of his remote cabin. The evidence is seen as crucial to the government's case against Kaczynski.
Kaczynski's lawyers had alleged that the search was illegal because an FBI affidavit supporting its request for a search warrant was misleading.

Earlier this month, Kaczynski's lawyers asked for permission to file another motion to suppress evidence seized during the cabin search on the grounds that the search warrant was too broad and that agents violated the scope of the warrant.

"Agents seized essentially everything in the cabin, including all of Mr. Kaczynski's personal papers, binders, notebooks and more than 200 books. Among the items seized ... were such innocuous items as kitchen knives, a blanket, a pillow, a container of Morton salt, fishing gear, and a can opener," the defence lawyers said in court papers. "They even collected dust and debris that had been vacuumed from the cabin floor," they said.
They argued that the warrant was so broad that it violated the Fourth Amendment's protections against unreasonable searches and seizures.
Burrell said he would allow defence lawyers to file the motion even though a filing deadline had passed. The prosecution has until Aug. 11 to file opposing arguments.
Burrell denied another defence motion to bar prosecutors from using Kaczynski's private diaries and other writings as evidence against him at trial.
Prosecutors have said that Kaczynski confessed to various bombings in the diaries.
Kaczynski's lawyers argued that use of the writings would violate Kaczynski's privacy rights and his constitutional rights against self-incrimination, among others.

But Burrell said the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination only applied when the government compelled someone to incriminate himself which had not been shown to have occurred in this case.
